meta.title: Why Do I Still Peek at My Ex's SNS After the Breakup?
meta.description: It's over — so why do you keep opening that profile? These 10 scenarios reveal the real reason you keep checking, and how to settle your heart.

startMessage.line1: It's over — so why do you keep opening that profile?
startMessage.line2: You swear you won't look, then your hand opens the app anyway. You know it'll tangle your feelings more, but it's hard to stop — and you catch yourself wondering if you're still hung up.
startMessage.line3: Behind what looks like "stalking" sits a different heart for everyone. Maybe you want proof they still think of you. Maybe you're comparing lives. Maybe checking soothes you. Maybe it's habit. Or maybe an unfinished story still needs a period. Naming it helps you sort it out.
startMessage.line4: These 10 scenarios show the real reason you keep checking — and how to settle your heart.

results.title: The One Who Wants to Know If You're Still on Their Mind, Lingering-Check Type 🔍
results.realReason: You want to know if you're still on their mind.
results.shortDescription: You're not stalking. You just want proof they still think about you — some lingering trace.
results.description: The wording of a new post, an account going private, a tiny profile change — each one feels like a signal aimed at you. Checking gives you a brief flicker of movement in your heart, but since there's never a clear answer, you end up going back in again. This feeling is proof that love still lingers, but it also burns a lot of energy on interpretation.
results.keywords: Looking for Clues, Reading Signals, Do They Think of Me, Unfinished Feelings, Overanalyzing
results.strengths: A deep heart that took the relationship seriously and doesn't erase people easily
results.reasonDetail: When you spot a new post, a profile change, or an active-status ping — or reopen your last chat
results.frequentSaying: "I wonder if they're still thinking about me."
results.changeTips:
When the urge to check hits, write down in one sentence what answer you're actually looking for.
Mute or hide their account so new notifications never reach your eyes.
Write two columns side by side: what you interpreted as a signal, and what's actually confirmed fact.
results.oneLiner: The more you read into clues, the bigger they grow. The answer isn't in their profile — it's in your own heart.
results.shareLine: Why do I still stalk my ex's SNS after the breakup? My result: Lingering-Check Type 🔍 Apparently I just want to know if they still think about me... this is SO me, I got chills. Saved it. What'd you get?

results.title: The One Who Puts Themselves and Their Ex on a Scale, Comparison Type ⚖️
results.realReason: You're measuring yourself by comparing your life to theirs.
results.shortDescription: You're not curious about them. You're placing your life next to theirs to measure where you stand.
results.description: A happy-looking photo, a hint of someone new, signs they're doing well — any of it can sink your mood. Comparison piles on top of heartbreak, and the thought "Am I the only one falling behind?" grows bigger. Checking their account rarely brings comfort — it usually just wears you out more.
results.keywords: Comparing Updates, Feeling Left Behind, Curious About Their New Person, Weighing Yourself, Self-Evaluation
results.strengths: Clear personal standards and a strong drive to keep growing and improving
results.reasonDetail: When you see a happy-looking post, or spot a clue they've started dating someone new
results.frequentSaying: "They're doing great and I'm the only one still a mess."
results.changeTips:
The moment comparison kicks in, write down three things you've accomplished this month.
Remember that what's posted online is just an edited highlight reel, not the full picture.
Swap your point of comparison from them to 'yourself a month ago' instead.
results.oneLiner: Their updates are the edited version; your heart is the original. Spend more time taking care of the original.

results.title: The One Who Soothes Themselves by Looking, Self-Comfort Type 🫶
results.realReason: Watching gives your mind a brief moment of ease — it's become a form of comfort.
results.shortDescription: You're not trying to deepen the wound. That account has quietly become a familiar comfort that soothes you.
results.description: Old photos, old messages, that familiar profile — they make you feel a little warmer, a little steadier. It's as if that account fills the empty space the breakup left behind. But the more you lean on it for comfort, the harder it gets to stop — and moving on gets pushed further back.
results.keywords: Comfort, Familiarity, Warm Memories, A Sense of Calm, Hard to Quit
results.strengths: A warmth that treasures good memories and knows how to soothe your own emotions
results.reasonDetail: On sleepless nights, when you feel hollow inside, or when old photos and messages come to mind
results.frequentSaying: "Looking at it just... makes me feel a little better."
results.changeTips:
For the hours you tend to need comfort (like at night), pre-plan a replacement routine — a walk, music, or calling a friend.
Keep the good memories in your own notes or photo album instead of on their account.
This week, make at least one real connection — with a friend or family member — where you can get comfort from an actual person.
results.oneLiner: Of course you need comfort. It's just that now, you're allowed to get it from the present version of yourself.
results.shareLine: Why do I still stalk my ex's SNS after the breakup? My result: Self-Comfort Type 🫶 Apparently checking became my go-to comfort routine... this is SO me, I got chills. Saved. What'd you get?

results.title: The One Whose Hand Moves First, Curiosity-Habit Type 📱
results.realReason: You open the app out of habit more than reason, just wanting to see what's new.
results.shortDescription: You might not even be going in because of lingering feelings. It's a repeated habit where your hand moves before your mind does.
results.description: When a new post shows up, you simply can't not look — and one post leads to the next, and the next. The scrolling has already started before you even figure out why. The small hit of stimulation each time you check has repeated into a loop that's hard to break.
results.keywords: Habit, Autopilot Scrolling, Curious About New Posts, Binge-Checking, Hard to Stop
results.strengths: Quick to pick up on new information and endlessly curious, which makes it easy for you to get absorbed in all kinds of things
results.reasonDetail: When a notification pops up, when you're mindlessly scrolling your phone, or in any idle, bored moment
results.frequentSaying: "I didn't even realize it — I was on their page again."
results.changeTips:
Move the app, or mute/block their account, to add extra steps before you can even open it.
When your hand reaches for it, do something else first for three minutes — drink water, stretch, anything.
Set a specific time of day for scrolling, and keep notifications off the rest of the time.
results.oneLiner: If it's your hand's habit rather than your heart, changing your environment is the fastest fix.
results.shareLine: Why do I still stalk my ex's SNS after the breakup? My result: Curiosity-Habit Type 📱 Apparently it's my hand that moves first, not my feelings... this is literally me LOL, saving this. What'd you get?

results.title: The One Whose Story Isn't Over Yet, Unfinished-Story Type 🧩
results.realReason: Unsaid words and unanswered questions are still hanging there — your heart hasn't gotten closure.
results.shortDescription: You don't actually miss them. It's an unfinished story still searching for its period.
results.description: Why it ended the way it did, what you never got to say, whether this breakup is really final — questions like these are still sitting in a corner of your heart. Opening their account is, in a way, an attempt to find the ending to that story. But the ending isn't written on their SNS — it's written in the sentences you put together yourself.
results.keywords: The Final Period, Words Left Unsaid, Unanswered Questions, An Awkward Ending, Searching for Closure
results.strengths: A conscientious drive to close relationships responsibly, and the will to actually work through your emotions
results.reasonDetail: When you remember your last conversation, recall the words you never said, or when the breakup finally feels real
results.frequentSaying: "I should have said that one thing before it ended."
results.changeTips:
Write the words you never said as a letter you'll never send — and finish it all the way through.
List out your unanswered questions, then sort them into 'ones I can answer myself' and 'ones only they would know.'
Pick a day to call it done, and treat muting or hiding their account that day as your official period.
results.oneLiner: The ending isn't something they hand you — it's something you write and close yourself. Line by line, the period eventually lands.
